doc_summary: Carlini argues that adversarial-defense evaluations are only meaningful if the evaluator actively and adaptively tries to break the specific defense, and gives concrete attack and sanity-check recommendations. He stresses that passing prior fixed attacks is weak evidence and that internal consistency checks reveal flawed evaluations.

items.claim: Prefers adaptive attacks written against the specific, fully specified defense over testing against previously known fixed attacks because a defense can trivially 'defeat' a fixed attack without being any more secure.
items.quote: a defense is only interesting from the perspective of a security evaluation if it withstands future attack. Showing that a defense can defeat previous attacks is a necessary, but not sufficient, component of an evaluation.

items.claim: Prefers asking 'what attack could possibly defeat this?' and showing every plausible attack fails over demonstrating success on a convenient benchmark, because the evaluator's job is to try to break the system.
items.quote: After the defense has been defined, ask: what attack could possibly defeat this defense? All attacks that might work must be shown to be ineffective.

items.claim: Prefers threat models that do not constrain the adversary's approach over arbitrary limits on attacker effort because there is no realistic reason an attacker could do 100 steps but not 1000.
items.quote: There is no reasonable threat model under which an attacker can compute 10 (or 100) iterations of gradient descent, but not 1000. Because the threat model must not constrain the approach an attacker takes, it is always worth evaluating against a strong attack

items.claim: Distrusts evaluations using weak or non-adaptive attacks (e.g., FGS only) because they can be passed via artifacts like gradient masking and give a false sense of robustness.
items.quote: It was never intended to be a strong attack for evaluating the robustness of a neural network, and should not be used as one.

items.claim: Uses internal-consistency sanity checks (iterative >= single-step, white-box >= black-box, monotonic in distortion, unbounded reaches 100%) to detect a flawed evaluation; violations signal a bug in the test rather than a real finding.
items.quote: Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, and so their results should be strictly superior. If an iterative attack performs worse than a single-step attack, this often indicates that the iterative attack is not correct.

items.claim: When a weaker method beats a stronger one (black-box beats white-box), investigate the specific instances where it did instead of dismissing it, since the anomaly reveals masking or a deficient attack.
items.quote: I suggest looking at which instances adversarial examples can be found with black-box but not white-box attacks. Check if these instances are at all related, and investigate why white-box attacks are not finding these adversarial examples.

items.claim: Collects evidence with diverse attack families (gradient-free, transfer, random search) to check the primary attack isn't missing something obvious, rather than relying on a single attack type.
items.quote: By attempting to generating adversarial examples with purely random search, by sampling completely random perturbations (with, e.g., Gaussian or uniform random noise) we can confirm that we aren't missing anything obvious.

items.claim: Prefers comparing methods under the same (strongest) evaluation over comparing numbers from mismatched evaluations because such comparisons are apples-to-oranges.
items.quote: if new defense A has 90% efficacy against some set of fixed attacks, but defense B has only 10% efficacy on adaptive attacks, it is no more fair to say “defense A is 80 percentage points more effective than B.”

items.claim: Prefers judging a defense by the worst-case attack over its average or best-case performance because a stronger attack's result supersedes weaker ones.
items.quote: It is important to compare defense against the worst attacks. If Defense A does better than Defense B on weaker attacks (e.g., FGS) but does worse against a stronger attack (e.g., PGD), then Defense B is the stronger defense.

items.claim: Treats weak evaluation as a field-wide problem rather than a problem of individual papers, and wants checklists useful to readers judging whether an evaluation is sufficient.
items.quote: it is not these papers, and these papers only, that were performing weak evaluations. The field as a whole is. These recommendations come from approaches I notice that we were taking that others were (are) not.
